title: Roushan's first song: the occasion
short: The young Roushan, son of the blinded master of the stud, sings this to the prince who blinded his father: a lesson in judging horses.
body: In Chodzko's Meeting I, Roushan's father Mirza-Serraf, master of the stud to Sultan Murad, presents two ugly colts sired by a stallion that rose out of the Oxus; the prince, insulted, has his eyes put out with a red-hot iron. The blind father raises one colt in a dark stable for forty days and trains it into a marvel. Roushan then rides out to meet the prince by the river and mocks him: 'thou believest thyself a good judge of horses'. This song is his lesson. Chodzko collected the cycle orally in northern Persia from professional singers and printed it in prose; the improvisations were in what he calls Perso-Turkish (Azerbaijani Turkish), and he gives no original of this one. In the Anatolian versions, as the TDV article summarises them, the tyrant is the Bey of Bolu and the father his groom (seyis).

title: The Prince
short: Sultan Murad, the ruler in Chodzko's version; the boast that the prince can learn from a boy reverses the power between them.
body: Chodzko names the ruler Sultan Murad, ruler of a province of Turkestan, who keeps Mirza-Serraf as Master of the Stud. In the Anatolian Köroğlu stories the tyrant is the Bey of Bolu, whose groom is blinded over a scrawny colt; Turkish scholarship from Pertev Naili Boratav (1931) onward treats these as branches of one tradition. The imperative 'listen and learn' is the heart of the insult: the ruler who prided himself on judging horses is sent back to school by the son of the man he maimed. The song is both instruction and revenge, as the narrative explains just before it: the father has told Roushan to show the prince the horse and bid him 'die of envy'.

anchor: a noble horse may be known
title: The noble horse and its signs
short: A catalogue of the points of a thoroughbred, treated in Persia, Chodzko says, as an authority to settle disputes about horses.
body: The song is a didactic catalogue of the 'signs' by which breeding shows, each organ compared to an animal: gazelle, chamois, camel, wolf, hare, peacock, serpent, eagle. Chodzko notes that Persian horse-connoisseurs attach great importance to this description and appeal to it in disputes over their racers; in his introduction he adds that the descriptions of Kyrat in Meetings I and V are considered the surest authority in questions of hippology. The horse is the true hero of the cycle: Chodzko says it is the only thing Kurroglou constantly loves, and the TDV article calls Kırat the hero's chief helper, a marvellous and tireless animal. The poem is a horse-praise, a genre also found in Arabic and Persian poetry.

title: The swelling nostrils
short: Wide, mobile nostrils, flaring and closing, were prized as signs of good wind and spirit in a horse.
body: The first point is breathing: the nostrils should swell and shrink rapidly in turn. Large, mobile nostrils were valued across the horse cultures of the Near East as a sign of good wind, the capacity to gallop far without tiring, and of high spirit; the Arabian horse is still bred and judged for them. 'Active and brisk' sums up the impression. Chodzko gives only a prose translation, but the list form suggests a catalogue a singer could expand or shorten at will. Compare the later song in the archive, 'A Noble Horse Walks Boldly', on a horse as fiery as its rider.

title: Gazelle, chamois, young camel
short: The legs of a gazelle poised to run, the haunches of a chamois, the soft mouth of a young camel: speed, spring and obedience.
body: Each comparison picks out one quality. The gazelle's slender legs, 'ready to commence its course', stand for speed and lightness; the gazelle (ceylan, ahu) is also the conventional image of beauty in Persian and Turkish love poetry, so the horse is praised in the language of the beloved. The chamois, a mountain goat-antelope, gives the powerful haunches needed for leaping over rocks, fitting a mountain bandit's horse. The 'tender mouth' that answers the slightest touch of the bridle, 'like the mouth of a young camel', means sensitivity to the rider's hand. Chodzko's 'chamois' may stand for some other wild mountain animal of Iran; the original is not given.

title: Millstone and wolf: the appetite
short: A good horse eats hungrily, grinding grain like a millstone and swallowing like a starving wolf: appetite as a sign of vigour.
body: A hearty appetite was taken as a sign of health and stamina: the horse grinds his barley so hard that it cracks 'like a millstone in motion' and bolts it like a hungry wolf. The wolf returns later in the song ('the restlessness of a hungry wolf') for the horse's eager, prowling walk. The animal is well chosen for a bandit's mount: the wolf, which hunts by night and lives by raiding, is the bandit's own emblem in Turkic tradition, and Kurroglou's raids on caravans are described in similar terms. The homely millstone shows the singer's pleasure in sound as well as sight.

title: The back of a hare
short: A short, strong, slightly arched back, like a hare's, built for sudden bursts of speed.
body: The hare's back is short, strong and slightly arched, the frame of an animal built for sprinting and sudden turns. Horsemen still prize a short, strong back for carrying weight and for quick acceleration. Chodzko's 'ought to remind you exactly' keeps the didactic tone: the song is a set of rules as well as a praise. The animal comparisons in the song are typical of the descriptive catalogues of Turkic oral epic, in which a hero's horse is often praised point by point.

anchor: formed in semblance of the peacock's
title: Silky mane, peacock neck
short: A soft mane and a high, arched neck carried like a peacock's: grace and pride of bearing.
body: The soft, silky mane and the 'lofty' neck carried in the curve of a peacock's describe the arched, proudly held neck admired in Persian and Turkmen horses. The peacock (tavus) is the emblem of beauty and display in Persian and Turkish poetry, and also, in Islamic legend, a bird of Paradise. The image moves the catalogue from function to beauty: a noble horse should be not only fast and strong but splendid to look at, fit for the parade before a prince.

anchor: between his fourth and fifth year
title: When to mount him
short: Practical horse-lore: the horse should be ridden in earnest between four and five years old, when its growth is complete.
body: The only plainly practical rule in the song: a horse should be mounted, that is broken and ridden hard, between his fourth and fifth year, when bones and joints are mature. Riding too young was held to ruin a horse. The rule fits the story: Roushan's colt is trained under strict conditions, forty nights over rocks and forty over marshes, a method Chodzko says the Turkmen used before a raid. Its presence shows that the song was valued, as Chodzko says, as a real authority on horses and not only as poetry.

title: chah-maur, the great serpent
short: Persian shah-mar, 'king of snakes', a large serpent: the horse's head should be neat and small like a snake's.
body: Chodzko leaves the word untranslated except as 'the great serpent'. It is evidently Persian shah-mar, literally 'king-snake' (shah, 'king', and mar, 'snake'), a name for a large serpent; the Turkish form şahmeran names the serpent-queen of Anatolian legend. The point of the comparison is a small, neat, finely shaped head, a mark of good breeding in Near Eastern horses. A snake's head is also alert and quick, so the image carries a hint of danger, apt for a war-horse.

title: Eyes like apples, teeth like diamonds
short: Large, prominent eyes and white, even teeth: the first are a mark of courage and intelligence in Near Eastern horse-lore.
body: Large, prominent eyes were valued in Arab and Persian horses as signs of courage, intelligence and good sight, and the comparison with 'two apples' gives their round fullness. 'Teeth like so many diamonds' moves from description into the jewelled hyperbole of praise poetry. Chodzko's introduction says that even exaggeration, the essential of Asiatic poetry in his view, is here comparatively sober; this catalogue mostly bears him out, its comparisons pointing to real features of a good horse.

title: Eagle eyes and the restless walk
short: Sharp, fierce eyes and a restless gait: the horse's spirit shows when it is brought out of the stable, playful and prancing.
body: After the static points the song turns to behaviour: brought out of the stable the horse is playful and prances, with the sharp gaze of an eagle and the restless walk of a hungry wolf. The eagle, a bird of prey and an emblem of sovereignty, matches the horse to its warrior rider; in the next song of the Meeting Roushan compares himself to a famished eagle refusing the prince's bait. A horse that fidgets with energy was preferred to a placid one; the later song in the archive, 'A Noble Horse Walks Boldly', praises a horse eager to throw its rider.

anchor: A young man of good family
title: The young man of good family
short: The catalogue turns from the horse to its owner: a well-born youth obeys his parents and cares for his horse and its pedigree.
body: Near the end the song shifts subject: the ideal is now the rider, a young man of good family who listens to his parents, tends his horse, knows its descent and 'pure blood' by heart, and tests the strength of its knees. Horse and master mirror each other; both are known by breeding and training. The lines also describe Roushan himself, an obedient son carrying out his blind father's instructions to the letter, and imply that the prince, who could not recognise a noble colt, lacks such knowledge. Pedigree was the pride of Turkmen horse-breeders, who kept the lines of their horses as carefully as their own.

title: Mirza-Serraf
greek: Persian mīrzā (from amīr-zāda, 'son of an emir')
short: Roushan's blinded father: the last line names him as the model horseman, which tells the prince who the singer is.
body: The last line, 'he ought to be what Mirza-Serraf was in his youth', is the sting of the song. It names the master of the stud whom the prince blinded for presenting the very colt now standing before him, and so reveals the singer's identity: the prince at once cries, 'This is the son of Mirza-Serraf. Ho, there! let him be arrested.' 'Mirza', from Persian amir-zada ('son of an emir'), was a title for a gentleman or secretary. In the story Mirza-Serraf is also a skilled astrologer who foresees his son's career. Roushan will soon take the name Kurroglou, 'son of the blind man' (Turkish kör, 'blind', oğlu, 'his son'), as Chodzko explains.
